documentation.range:
This species ranges throughout much of the Mediterranean region. Mainland European subpopulations are distributed from Portugal (where it occurs countrywide), Spain (where it is absent from most of the north), and southern France, throughout mainly coastal areas of Italy, southern Slovenia (from which there is a single observation - Szabolcs et al. 2021), northern coastal Croatia, which appears to represent the eastern limit of its assumed native range in Europe (Midtgaard 2019). Its true native range is, however, unclear, and low genetic diversity across Europe may indicate that it is introduced in at least parts of its European range (Rato et al. 2016), potentially including areas where it is presently treated as native. It occurs disjunctly in the Balkans in Albania and southwest Greece, with a dubious report from Montenegro, and reports of individual animals from Bulgaria where it is unclear if any established populations exist (Speybroeck et al. 2016, Mizsei et al. 2017, Szabolcs et al. 2021, Jablonski et al. 2022), and available evidence suggests that most if not all Balkan populations result from introductions (Szabolcs et al. 2021, Jablonski et al. 2022, Harris et al. 2024). Northward range expansion in France may be a response to climate warming (Geniez and Cheylan 2012).

In northern Africa the species ranges throughout the Mahgreb from northwestern Western Sahara and Morocco (where it occurs across most of the country, south to around the Oued Dráa - Martínez del Mármol et al. 2019), the Spanish North African territories (Bacallado Aránega et al. 2012), through northern Algeria to northern Tunisia and Lampudesa (Italy). In Morocco, which has the highest number of Tarentola species in the world, it is replaced in some areas with related species (G. Martínez del Mármol pers. comm. 2024).

Many of the subpopulations in the northern Mediterranean are likely to have been introduced in ancient times. Genetic evidence indicates that the highest diversity, and likely the natural origin, of the species lies in Morocco and the Iberian Peninsula. European subpopulations elsewhere appear to result from ancient introductions, more recent secondary introductions from established Italian subpopulations, or from a combination of these two invasion routes (Rato et al. 2023). Whether it has a native or introduced origin in Sardinia and Sicily, or in North Africa east of Morocco, is unclear (Rato et al. 2023). More recent introductions have been documented in the Balearic Islands (Spain), Madeira and the Azores (Portugal), Montevideo (Uruguay), Buenos Aires (Argentina) and California (United States). A record from Daklha in Western Sahara south of the known native range presumably represents an introduction, and the population here may be extinct (Martínez del Mármol et al. 2019). It is possible that some Libyan records assigned to Tarentola fascicularis by Bauer et al. (2017) represent introduced populations of the Moorish Gecko.

It is found from sea level up to 2,300 m asl (in Spain) and 2,500 (in Morocco), though is usually found below 400 m asl (Speybroeck et al. 2016, Martínez del Mármol et al. 2019). It is likely that climate change will allow the species to expand its elevational range (G. Martínez del Mármol pers. comm. 2025).
documentation.population: This species is abundant throughout its range, especially on islands (Speybroeck et al. 2016). It is the most easily found member of the genus in both Andalusia and many areas of Morocco, especially in rocky areas where it colonises vertical surfaces of buildings (G. Martínez del Mármol pers. comm. 2025). Subpopulations may be expanding with increasing urbanisation.
documentation.habitats: It is found in a variety of habitats, from scrubland and dry maquis to bare rock faces, and it has been recorded from rocky areas, cliffs, stone walls, ruins, building walls and inside houses (where it can be abundant) (Speybroeck et al. 2016). It can also be common in forests or plantations, including those characterised by cork oak or olive trees (G. Martínez del Mármol pers. comm. 2025). It can be found "essentially anywhere where there are appropriate crevices to use as refugia" (Martínez del Mármol et al. 2019). Its only limiting factor appears to be elevation (G. Martínez del Mármol pers. comm. 2025). It is generally not present in forested areas although animals can often be found climbing in trees. The females lay clutches of one to two eggs. These may be laid communally, typically under stones, in cracks and in hollow trees. Females may lay several clutches a year (Speybroeck et al. 2016).
documentation.threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. Subpopulations in Egypt may be locally threatened by overcollection for the pet trade and by habitat degradation (S. Baha El Din pers. comm.).
documentation.measures: It is protected by international legislation over parts of its range, and it occurs in many protected areas. Further studies into the impact of commercial trade on this species in Egypt is needed. Further taxonomic studies are needed for this species.
documentation.use_trade: There is at least localised collection of this species in part of its range for the pet trade.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
The highly complex taxonomy of the Tarentola mauritanica group poses a "particular problem", and is summarised by Bauer et al. (2017). The genetically distinct North African form T. m. fascicularis was considered a subspecies until it was elevated to specific status by Joger and Bshaenia (2010). Trape et al. (2012) continued to treat T. fascicularis as a subspecies of T. mauritanica and this concept was followed in a previous Red List assessment (Vogrin et al. 2017), however, the current assessment follows recent papers and Uetz et al. (2023) in accepting T. fascicularis as a distinct species.

A lack of concordance with nuclear DNA has however limited progress on clarifying the taxonomy of this group (Rato et al. 2016), and range limits remain poorly understood.
